Policy Name/Title: National Guidance for the Responsible and Safe Use of Artificial Intelligence in Health and Social Care Services
Summary: Provides national operational guidance for responsible and safe AI use across Irish health and social care, organized around accountability, a human rights-based approach, safety and wellbeing, and responsiveness, with practical expectations for governance, transparency, human oversight, data quality, workforce preparation, and monitoring.
Healthcare Implications: Health and social care services should establish accountable oversight, approved-use policies, and clear roles; preserve human judgment and informed participation; protect privacy and equity; train staff; evaluate safety and accuracy; and maintain incident, downtime, and withdrawal processes throughout deployment.

Policy Name/Title: National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 (AI Nation 2030)
Issuing Body: Ministry of Digital; AI Malaysia Berhad (National AI Office)
Summary: Sets Malaysia's national AI implementation agenda through sectoral Impact Engines and system-wide governance. Its Ministry of Health-led healthcare engine calls for locally validated AI diagnostics, population-health and noncommunicable-disease surveillance, AI-generated patient summaries, and AI-enabled clinical research, while the plan proposes a hybrid risk-based governance framework with central coordination and sector-regulator authority.
Healthcare Implications: Health agencies, hospitals, and developers are directed toward phased deployment of AI in radiology, pathology, cardiology, preventive care, and clinical research using national health data and local validation. The plan is strategic rather than binding, but it creates a national delivery and governance structure for scaling healthcare AI.

Policy Name/Title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 – Artificial Intelligence Act, as Amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
Issuing Body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
Summary: Updates the European Union’s horizontal, risk-based AI law through the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI, clarifying implementation and conformity pathways, revising selected governance and transparency provisions, and changing the application timetable for high-risk AI requirements.
Healthcare Implications: Medical-device and in vitro diagnostic AI remains subject to coordinated AI Act and MDR or IVDR compliance. Chapter III high-risk duties now apply on 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I product systems, requiring vendors and healthcare deployers to update conformity, documentation, data-governance, human-oversight, and post-market plans.

Policy Name/Title: General Principles on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Preparation of the JCA Dossier
Issuing Body: Member State Coordination Group on Health Technology Assessment
Summary: Establishes principles for using artificial intelligence to prepare evidence for EU Joint Clinical Assessment dossiers. Preserves health technology developers’ accountability for dossier content and methods, requires appropriate human oversight, and calls for transparent documentation of AI-assisted activities, including the tools, versions, purposes, steps, and outputs involved.
Healthcare Implications: Pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and medical-device developers using AI to prepare EU health technology assessment submissions should maintain human control, validate AI-assisted evidence work, document how and where AI was used, preserve methodological rigor, and comply with applicable data-protection, copyright, AI Act, and health technology assessment requirements.

Policy Name/Title: Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All
Summary: Establishes a five-year national AI strategy organized around trust, opportunity, and sovereignty. Its first sector mission commits to AI-enabled health and life sciences through a national Health Sector Data Space and expansion of the VITAL clinical-data platform, alongside broader privacy, safety, transparency, and sovereign-infrastructure measures.
Healthcare Implications: Creates a nationally backed pathway for health systems and researchers to connect standardized health datasets while participating organizations retain data stewardship, supporting AI research, clinical trials, validation, and health-system analysis. The strategy funds infrastructure and governance capacity but does not impose direct duties on providers or developers.

Policy Name/Title: WHA79.9 – Strengthening Equitable Access to Diagnostic Imaging Through Teleradiology
Summary: Formal World Health Assembly resolution urging Member States to integrate teleradiology into national health, digital health, and diagnostic strategies; develop or strengthen national policies, standards, and regulatory frameworks for safe and ethical teleradiology; and support the safe, trustworthy, accurate, robust, and ethical use of artificial intelligence and decision-support tools in teleradiology workflows with appropriate validation, transparency, human oversight, data governance, privacy, and equity considerations.
Healthcare Implications: Provides a global health-policy signal for AI-enabled diagnostic imaging and teleradiology. It is relevant to governments, health systems, radiology services, and developers because it links AI decision-support tools in teleradiology to validation, clinical oversight, transparency, privacy, data governance, equity, interoperability, and future WHO normative guidance.

Policy Name/Title: Artificial Intelligence Information Governance Guidance for Health and Care
Summary: Provides a linked suite of guidance for patients, health and care professionals, and information-governance teams on lawful and safe data use in AI, covering data-protection impact assessments, legal bases, controller and processor roles, data minimization, accuracy, fairness, transparency, security, and automated decision-making.
Healthcare Implications: Health and care organizations should complete a data-protection impact assessment before implementing AI, document legal bases and responsibilities, assess data quality and unfair effects, provide clear information to patients and staff, apply data-minimization and security controls, and retain meaningful human review for consequential uses.

Healthcare Implications: The policy gives federal direction for AI adoption across the UAE health sector and for a future law addressing development, licensing, accreditation, operation, data governance, safety and quality, liability, patient rights, and federal-local coordination. Summary: Examines the opportunities, risks, and governance needs associated with using artificial intelligence throughout evidence-informed health policymaking. Maps AI use across problem definition, policy design, implementation, monitoring, and adjustment and discusses impact assessments, readiness reviews, human verification, human decision gateways, multidisciplinary oversight, transparency, participation, and rights protections.
Healthcare Implications: Health ministries, public-health agencies, regulators, and health-policy organizations can use the paper to inform governance of AI-assisted evidence retrieval, synthesis, forecasting, policy analysis, implementation, and monitoring. Policy Name/Title: Guidance on the Use of AI-Enabled Ambient Scribing Products in Health and Care Settings, Version 2
Summary: Provides national implementation guidance for health and care organizations adopting generative-AI ambient-scribing products. Version 2 aligns the guidance with the NHS Ambient Voice Technology Supplier Registry and addresses clinical-safety leadership, safety cases and hazard logs, data-protection impact assessments, medical-device status, procurement, system integration, piloting, human review, staff training, performance monitoring, bias, and supplier assurance.
Healthcare Implications: NHS organizations adopting AI scribes should establish clinical-safety and information-governance controls, require users to review and approve outputs, assess regulatory status, integrate products safely with patient records, independently monitor accuracy and incidents, evaluate performance across patient populations and speech characteristics, and ensure suppliers meet national and local assurance requirements.

Policy Name/Title: Position Statement: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Pharmacy
Summary: Applies existing professional, pharmacy, education, and revalidation standards to the use of artificial intelligence. States that pharmacy professionals remain personally accountable for AI-assisted decisions and should understand system limitations, review outputs for accuracy and bias, be transparent with patients, protect confidential information, obtain consent where necessary, and not allow AI to replace professional judgment.
Healthcare Implications: Pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, and pharmacy owners should establish due-diligence, governance, risk-assessment, data-protection, training, human-review, and monitoring controls for AI. Registered pharmacies may need to demonstrate these controls during inspections, and unsafe or inappropriate AI use may be addressed through existing investigation and fitness-to-practise processes.

Policy Name/Title: Interim Measures for the Management of Anthropomorphic AI Interactive Services
Issuing Body: Cyberspace Administration of China; National Development and Reform Commission; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; Ministry of Public Security; State Administration for Market Regulation
Summary: Establishes binding rules for public-facing AI services that simulate human personality, communication style, and sustained emotional interaction. Covered providers must maintain lifecycle safety controls, protect user privacy and interaction data, label AI-generated interactions, limit overdependence and addictive use, intervene in extreme emotional or life-threatening self-harm situations, add protections for minors and older adults, conduct safety assessments in specified circumstances, and comply with algorithm filing and regulatory supervision requirements.
Healthcare Implications: Highly relevant to mental-health-adjacent AI companions and emotional-support chatbots. The measures create direct safety, disclosure, data-protection, youth-safety, and crisis-response obligations for emotionally interactive AI services and require health-related uses to comply with relevant health-sector rules. Developers of AI companions, virtual care assistants, and behavioral-health support tools operating in China must account for psychological-risk monitoring, emergency-contact workflows, limits on minor-facing intimate services, usage-duration reminders, AI labeling, sensitive interaction-data limits, and regulatory safety assessments.

Policy Name/Title: Pre-market Guidance for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices
Summary: Health Canada guidance for manufacturers submitting new or amendment applications for Class II, III, and IV machine-learning-enabled medical devices. The guidance explains MLMD scope, risk classification, lifecycle evidence expectations, good machine learning practice, design, risk management, data selection and management, development and training, testing and evaluation, clinical validation, transparency, post-market monitoring, and predetermined change control plans.
Healthcare Implications: Canadian sponsors and manufacturers of ML-enabled medical devices should structure premarket submissions and lifecycle documentation around Health Canada’s expectations for safety and effectiveness, representative datasets, SGBA Plus, transparency, PCCPs, change management, and post-market monitoring. Health systems and purchasers can use the guidance as a reference for vendor diligence and deployment-risk review.

Issuing Body: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
Summary: Health-specific AI policy checklist developed by the OECD with the Global Digital Health Partnership, Coalition for Health AI, and OECD AI in Health Expert Group. Policy Name/Title: Guidance on Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Patient Care
Summary: Professional guidance for doctors using AI in patient care. The guidance covers AI embedded in medical devices, AI scribes, AI tools that manage clinical inboxes, and AI systems that influence clinical decisions. It states that doctors remain responsible for clinical decisions and actions, must understand AI capabilities and limitations, check AI outputs where reasonably practicable, document AI use when it influences clinical decision-making, avoid using AI to impersonate themselves, inform patients when AI is used in care, obtain informed consent in specified higher-risk uses, and ensure privacy, data security, safety, and fairness.
Healthcare Implications: Creates a practical professional-responsibility framework for AI use by New Zealand doctors. It directly affects clinical deployment of AI scribes, decision-support tools, inbox-management systems, and AI-enabled devices by emphasizing clinician accountability, patient transparency, consent, documentation, privacy safeguards, data security, suitability for the patient population, and avoidance of bias or worsening inequities. It is guidance rather than legislation, but it gives clear expectations for safe and ethical AI use in patient-facing medical practice.

Issuing Body: Ministry of Health Singapore; Health Sciences Authority
Summary: Updated national guidance for the safe and responsible development, deployment, and use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. AIHGle 2.0 clarifies that AI should augment healthcare professionals, addresses generative AI and other developments, clarifies stakeholder responsibilities for developers, deployers, and healthcare professional users, and adds guidance on transparency, risk assessment, mitigation, and deployment governance.

It is voluntary guidance, but it complements HSA software-as-medical-device regulation and should shape institutional AI governance, procurement, disclosure, risk-management, and deployment-review workflows.

Policy Name/Title: CFM Resolution No. 2.454/2026 – Use of Artificial Intelligence in Medicine
Issuing Body: Federal Council of Medicine (Conselho Federal de Medicina)
Summary: Regulates the use of artificial intelligence in medical practice in Brazil. The resolution treats AI as a support tool for medical practice, clinical decision-making, health management, research, and education; requires physicians to remain finally responsible for clinical, diagnostic, therapeutic, and prognostic decisions; requires patient disclosure when AI is used as relevant support in care, diagnosis, or treatment; requires preliminary risk classification, governance processes, human supervision, data protection, monitoring, and bias-mitigation measures for medical AI systems.
Healthcare Implications: Creates one of the clearest physician-facing AI governance frameworks in the international module. Brazilian physicians and medical institutions using or developing AI must preserve physician autonomy and final medical judgment, explain AI use to patients, document AI use in medical records when used for decision support, avoid delegating diagnosis or therapeutic communication to AI without human mediation, classify AI systems by risk, and implement internal governance and oversight for safety, quality, ethics, privacy, security, and bias mitigation.

Policy Name/Title: Health Products (AI Standalone Mobile Application — Exemption) Order 2026 / AI-SaMD Sandbox
Issuing Body: Health Sciences Authority; Government of Singapore
Summary: Creates a regulatory sandbox exemption for qualifying artificial-intelligence software as a medical device developed by selected public healthcare entities for use in public healthcare. The exemption relieves covered AI-SaMD from manufacturer licensing and product registration requirements, subject to safeguards including Class A or B scope, non-critical medical-condition use, clinician oversight, yearly ISO 13485 QMS self-attestation, senior institutional endorsement, HSA pre-deployment notification, patient notification, post-market obligations, and enforcement for breaches.
Healthcare Implications: Enables selected Singapore public healthcare institutions to deploy lower-risk AI-SaMD under controlled conditions while maintaining clinical oversight, quality-system expectations, patient notice, HSA visibility, adverse-event reporting, and enforcement. Developers and health systems outside the selected public-healthcare pathway should treat this as a limited regulatory sandbox, not a general AI-SaMD market-access exemption.

Summary: Explains when AI or software is regulated as a medical device in Australia and how intended purpose, risk classification, evidence, conformity assessment, Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods inclusion, and lifecycle obligations apply.
Healthcare Implications: Manufacturers and sponsors should determine whether AI functions meet the medical-device definition, assign the correct classification, and meet Essential Principles, quality, clinical-evidence, cybersecurity, change-control, and post-market obligations. Policy Name/Title: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust
Issuing Body: South Korean Ministry of Government Legislation
Summary: South Korea’s comprehensive national AI law, enacted in 2025 and enforced beginning January 22, 2026. The Act defines high-impact AI to include AI used in systems for providing and using healthcare services and AI used in the development and use of medical devices or digital medical devices. It establishes national AI governance structures, transparency duties for high-impact and generative AI, safety and risk-management expectations, confirmation procedures for high-impact AI classification, user protection measures, human management and supervision, documentation duties, and impact-assessment encouragement.
Healthcare Implications: Healthcare and medical-device AI are expressly included within the Act’s high-impact AI framework, making the law relevant to Korean health systems, medical AI developers, and digital medical device companies. Operators of healthcare AI may need to assess whether systems qualify as high-impact AI, notify users that products or services are AI-based, maintain risk-management and user-protection measures, support explainability where technically feasible, retain safety/reliability documentation, and preserve human management and supervision. Certified digital medical products may also interact with the Act’s deemed-compliance/safe-harbor structure.
